one_liner: Public-domain asynchronous C++ logger with crash-safe flush; ~3x lower call-site latency than Boost.Log, 3-4x slower than spdlog.
what_it_does: g3log moves file I/O off the calling thread: LOG(level) << ... (stream) and LOGF(level, fmt, ...) (printf-style) build the message at the call site and hand it to a background LogWorker that forwards it to one or more sinks. It also provides CHECK/CHECK_F design-by-contract macros and installs handlers for SIGABRT, SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGSEGV and SIGTERM that flush every queued message, plus a stack dump, before the process dies. Setup is explicit (createLogWorker, addDefaultLogger or addSink, initializeLogging); it is not an API drop-in for Boost.Log, glog or iostreams.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing is written to disk on the caller's thread: LogCapture formats into a std::ostringstream, copies the text into a heap-allocated LogMessage (timestamp, thread id, file, function) and pushes a std::function onto an Active object, a mutex-protected unbounded std::queue with a condition variable (shared_queue.hpp). The LogWorker thread then posts the message to each sink's own Active thread, and the default FileSink appends to a string buffer and flushes the std::ofstream every 100 messages. This beats loggers that format and write synchronously or take heavier locks, but every call still pays iostream formatting, two or more allocations, a mutex and a notify, about 1 us on a modern core.
when_to_use: Applications that need the last log lines before a crash: queued messages and a stack dump reach the sink on SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGTERM, LOG(FATAL) or a failed CHECK.
Moderate log rates (thousands to low hundreds of thousands of messages per second) where roughly 1 us per call is acceptable and disk stalls must not block the caller.
Replacing Boost.Log, glog-style synchronous logging or std::fstream with a flush per line in code that already uses stream-style LOG(INFO) << syntax.

Projects that want public-domain (Unlicense) source with no third-party dependency for the default file sink, plus custom sinks (log rotation, syslog, colour terminal in g3sinks) added or removed at run time.
when_not_to_use: Latency-critical hot paths: in the Quill benchmark g3log's median call is 1066 ns (1 thread) and 1188 ns (4 threads), versus 271/557 ns for spdlog and 6-29 ns for fmtlog, Quill, XTR, PlatformLab NanoLog and binlog.

Bursty high-volume logging: the queue is an unbounded mutex-protected std::queue with no back-pressure or drop policy, so memory grows while the sink falls behind, and all messages pass through one LogWorker thread.

Processes that own their signal handling (PID 1, JVM or Python hosts, crash reporters, sanitizers): g3log installs its own fatal handlers by default, treats SIGTERM as fatal, and re-raises the signal after restoring the previous handler; disable it with ENABLE_FATAL_SIGNALHANDLING=OFF or overrideSetupSignals.
Programs that leave through exit() or need structured or binary logs: the docs state queued entries are not flushed on exit(), and output is plain text only.

integration.form: static or shared lib (CMake; G3_SHARED_LIB defaults ON)
integration.dependencies: none for the default file sink (C++ standard library and pthreads); extra sinks live in KjellKod/g3sinks
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (MSVC and MinGW) per docs/building.md; iOS build option; fatal-signal handling is POSIX-signal based on Unix and vectored exceptions on Windows
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe LOG calls from any thread (docs/API.md); initialize the logger before other threads log and destroy it after they stop

gotchas: The fatal-signal handler is not async-signal-safe: it builds std::ostringstream text, calls backtrace_symbols and pushes the message through the same mutex queue, so a crash inside malloc or while a thread holds the queue lock can hang instead of flushing.

Messages logged before initializeLogging are dropped; only the first one is printed to stderr as 'LOGGER NOT INITIALIZED'. Run-time level filtering needs USE_DYNAMIC_LOGGING_LEVELS=ON (default OFF), and the DEBUG level name can clash with other macros unless CHANGE_G3LOG_DEBUG_TO_DBUG=ON.
Each sink runs its own background thread in addition to the LogWorker thread, so the default setup creates two threads, and messages hop two mutex queues before reaching the file.

Benchmark harness flaw in the baseline: logger_benchmarks' Boost.Log harness shares one non-thread-safe src::severity_logger across all caller threads (Boost.Log documents the _mt variants as the thread-safe ones), so the 4-thread Boost.Log rows measure a data race; the 1-thread comparison (g3log about 2.9-3.2x lower latency) is unaffected.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick g3log over glog or loguru when you want logging off the caller's thread plus crash-time flushing and CHECK macros in a public-domain, dependency-free package; if call-site latency matters, Quill (which also lists a built-in crash signal handler), fmtlog or binlog run at 6-29 ns in the same harness and Iyengar NanoLog at 106 ns, 10-170x below g3log's 1066 ns median.
verified_claims_summary: In odygrd/logger_benchmarks (Quill v13.0.0 README tables; GCC 14.2, -m64 -march=x86-64-v3, C++20, Intel Core i5-12600 with isolated cores), g3log's LOG(INFO) to its default file sink took 1066/1095/1143 ns at the 50th/90th/99.9th percentile versus 3093/3259/3621 ns for Boost.Log's asynchronous text sink with one caller thread (about 2.9-3.2x lower, derived from page data), and 838 versus 2844 ns at the median for large strings; g3log was slower than spdlog and every other logger in those tables. The reckless benchmark (gcc 7.3.0, Ryzen 7 2700X, g3log 1.3.2) shows g3log far below std::fstream with a flush per line under heavy disk I/O but slower than stdio fprintf+fflush.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-04, 965 stars, no open issues listed), Unlicense public domain with no patent grant, and a small dependency-free codebase that is easy to vendor; its queue design dates from 2010 and has not been modernised for low latency.
